newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Foreign unionists complain of S.Korean harassment.
newsitem.headline: Foreign unionists complain of S.Korean harassment.

text.p: International labour leaders visiting South Korea to show solidarity with strikers accused the governmnent on Wednesday of intimidation after they were visited by immigration police.
At a news conference, they also appealed to authorities not to carry out threats to arrest union heads and warned that South Korea's reputation would suffer if there was a crackdown.

The four-man mission has irked the government with regular visits to Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral where strike leaders are sheltering from arrest and by appearing as star guests at several worker rallies.
Local media reports said the four risked deportation, although there was no official comment.

Marcello Malentacchi, head of the International Metalworkers' Federation, said immigration police had visited members of the delegation on Monday evening at their hotel and warned they were violating the terms of their visas by engaging in political activities.
"The government is just trying to intimidate the mission," he said, sporting a read headband inscribed with the Korean word for "fight".
John Evans, head of a union advisory committee to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), said Seoul would pay a price for any repressive measures.
"If there is a crackdown it would be an embarrassment for the Korean government in the OECD which won't go away for a long time," he said.
South Korea formally joined the Paris-based organisation last month.
The OECD is holding a meeting on January 22 to review South Korea's new labour law that has sparked three weeks of strikes.
South Korea's partners in the OECD have expressed concern that the new law violates worker rights to freedom of expression by maintaining a ban on new labour union bodies until 2000.
The only legitimate union group is the Federation of Korean Trade Unions. The militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, whose leaders are evading arrest, is outlawed.

"I have never experienced in my trade union life this kind of government authority interfering in our stay and our business," said Takashi Izumi, Singapore-based representative of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU).
"I don't think we have violated any law."
The fourth member of the delegation, which arrived on Saturday to investigate labour strife, is Guy Ryder, Director of the Geneva office of the ICFTU.
The four have attracted intense media attention and on Wednesday many newpapers led their front pages with government warnings against the visitors.
The Dong-a Ilbo said authorities "would use deportation as a final means".
On Tuesday the Korea Herald quoted ruling New Korea Party chairman Lee Hong-koo as criticising the confederation for teaming up with foreign labour groups.
"We must solve our problems for ourself, through dialogue and debate," he was quoted as saying, referring to the four as "foreigners whose identities are ambiguous".
The visiting unionists said said they received no written communication from the government.
